excerpt: Upholstery and cubicle panel steam cleaning is priced per chair, per square foot of fabric, or per specialty hour, and the unit you choose changes the total. This guide gives US office managers national ranges, minimum charges, and a worked example for a typical cubicle floor.
quickAnswer: Nationally, hot-water extraction of office upholstery runs about $12–$30 per task chair, $25–$60 per executive or lounge chair, and $0.60–$1.25 per sq ft of fabric panel face, or $55–$95 per specialty labor hour. Most vendors enforce a $90–$135 minimum per visit, and many set a higher project minimum of $175–$250 for a full extraction setup. For a 50-workstation cubicle floor, cleaning all seating plus the inside faces of the panels typically lands between $3,100 and $6,900.

blocks.text: The three pricing units vendors use for upholstery and panel cleaning

Unlike nightly janitorial service, which is quoted per square foot of floor area, upholstery and fabric panel steam cleaning is priced by the thing being cleaned. Vendors use one of three units: per piece for chairs and lounge seating, per square foot of fabric face for cubicle panels and acoustic wall wraps, or per specialty labor hour for mixed jobs. Knowing which unit a vendor is quoting is the only way to compare bids, because a low per-chair price can hide a high panel rate or an inflated minimum.

The process itself is consistent: dry soil removal with a HEPA vacuum and upholstery tool, pre-spray with a fabric-safe cleaning solution, dwell time, then hot-water extraction with a hand tool and a final grooming pass. Many vendors call this steam cleaning even though the water is typically heated to 180°F–210°F rather than true vapor steam.

blocks.title: How to sanity-check a per-hour quote
blocks.text: A trained tech extracts roughly 4 to 7 standard task chairs per hour. At $55–$95 per hour that implies $8–$24 per chair, consistent with per-piece pricing. If an hourly quote implies a much higher per-chair figure, ask for the vendor's production rate assumption.

Panel pricing causes the most confusion because vendors measure differently. Some quote linear feet of panel run, some quote the face area of one side, and some quote both sides. A standard 5 ft wide by 5 ft tall panel has 25 sq ft per face, or 50 sq ft if both sides are fabric. A typical 6 ft by 6 ft workstation with three fabric panels at 5 ft height has roughly 90 sq ft of single-side fabric face, though shared walls between adjacent stations reduce the per-station total on a floor.

items: Ask whether the quote counts one face or both; inside faces get dirtier, outside faces along aisles get scuffed.
Exclude glass or laminate upper tiles, which are wiped rather than extracted.
Count shared spine walls once, not once per workstation.
Confirm whether tackable fabric with pinholes or tape residue is priced at the standard rate or a spot-treatment rate.

blocks.text: Consider a 12,000 sq ft office with 50 workstations, 50 fabric task chairs, 20 conference chairs, and a reception area with four lounge chairs and one sofa. Shared panels produce about 3,000 sq ft of single-side fabric face, and the client wants both sides cleaned, or 6,000 sq ft total.

blocks.caption: Illustrative estimate for a 50-workstation, 12,000 sq ft office

blocks.text: Most offices do not extract every panel face annually. A common approach is to clean all chairs and only the inside faces of panels, which here would be roughly 3,000 sq ft and bring the full job to about $3,130–$6,930. Many buyers clean chairs every year and panels every second year, which spreads the inside-face panel cost over two years and keeps the annual average near $2,200–$5,100 for this floor.
What drives the price up or down

items: Volume: jobs above 100 chairs often earn a 10% to 25% unit discount because setup and travel are spread across more pieces.
Access: after-hours or weekend work to avoid disrupting staff can add a 10% to 20% premium.
Fabric type: wool blends, microsuede, or fabrics coded S (solvent clean only) require low-moisture or solvent methods and cost more.
Soil and stains: coffee, ink, and makeup spotting adds time; heavy stain lists may be billed hourly.
Water and power: dedicated outlets and a nearby utility sink keep heated equipment running without interruptions.

blocks.title: Check the fabric cleaning code first
blocks.text: Manufacturer tags use W (water-based), S (solvent only), W/S (either), and X (vacuum only). Extracting an S-coded chair with hot water can cause rings, shrinkage, or dye bleed. Require the vendor to inventory codes before quoting and to exclude or reprice S and X items.
Equipment a qualified vendor should bring

Ask what extractor the vendor will use. For chairs and panel spotting, a compact heated unit such as the Powr-Flite PE301 heated spotter (3-gallon tank, 60 PSI pump, 10 ft hose) is common. For larger panel runs and mid-size suites, a higher-pressure unit like the Mytee Lite 8070 (4-gallon tank, 120 PSI, 1000W in-line heat, 4-inch upholstery tool) recovers more moisture, which shortens dry time. Faster drying matters: panels and seats should be usable within 2 to 6 hours, and moisture left in foam can cause odors. If the vendor also refreshes hard floors in the same visit, an orbital such as the Bissell Commercial BGEM9000, a 13-inch random-orbit, low-vibration machine on a 50 ft cord, handles VCT and tile around the workstations.

items.name: Inventory pieces and fabric codes
items.text: Count chairs by type and record W, S, W/S, or X tags; measure panel faces and note shared walls.

items.name: Request quotes in the same unit
items.text: Ask every vendor for per-chair and per-sq-ft pricing plus the minimum charge, so bids line up.

items.name: Confirm process and dry time
items.text: Require pre-vacuuming, documented chemical dilution with SDS on file, and a target dry time under 6 hours.

items.name: Schedule and verify
items.text: Book outside business hours, spot-check a sample of chairs and panels the next morning, and hold payment until any re-treat items are resolved.

faqs.q: What is a fair price to steam clean one office chair?
faqs.a: For a standard fabric task chair, $12–$30 is the typical national range, with mesh-back chairs at the low end and fully upholstered executive or conference chairs at $25–$60. Expect a minimum visit charge of $90–$135, so very small orders often cost more per chair.

faqs.q: Is panel cleaning priced by linear foot or square foot?
faqs.a: Most vendors price by square foot of fabric face at about $0.60–$1.25, but some quote linear feet of panel run. Convert linear feet by multiplying by panel height, and confirm whether one or both faces are included before comparing bids.

faqs.q: What chemicals and safety documents should the vendor provide?
faqs.a: The vendor should keep Safety Data Sheets for pre-sprays, spotters, and rinses under OSHA HazCom and train techs on them. For occupied offices, ask for low-VOC or Green Seal certified upholstery products, and confirm that any spotting involving blood or bodily fluids follows OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens procedures.

faqs.q: How long do chairs and panels take to dry?
faqs.a: With a well-maintained heated extractor and good airflow, fabric typically dries in 2 to 6 hours. Schedule work for evenings or Friday nights, run HVAC fans, and avoid sitting on seats until they are dry to the touch to prevent re-soiling.

faqs.q: Should the vendor's insurance cover fabric damage?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask for a certificate of insurance showing general liability with your company named as additional insured, and confirm the policy does not exclude damage to property in the vendor's care. Fabric shrinkage or dye bleed on executive chairs is a realistic claim scenario.
